column3: According to the README of the Rust project's RFC repository, the "RFC" (request for comments) process provides a consistent and controlled path for changes to Rust, such as new features, so that all stakeholders can be confident about the direction of the project. Many changes can go through the normal GitHub pull request workflow, while "substantial" changes are put through a design process and need consensus among the Rust community and the sub-teams. To get a major feature added, the author first gets the RFC merged into the RFC repository as a markdown file, and the RFC then becomes "active" and may be implemented. A sub-team member proposes a motion for final comment period with a disposition of merge, close or postpone, and that period lasts ten calendar days so that it is open for at least five business days. The README says being "active" is not a rubber stamp, and that once accepted RFCs should not be substantially changed: more substantial changes should be new RFCs, with a note added to the original.
